title: Good faith estimates for uninsured and self-pay clients (No Surprises Act)
summary: Under the federal No Surprises Act, health care providers, including licensed mental health clinicians, must give uninsured clients and clients who choose not to use insurance a written good faith estimate of expected charges before scheduled services or on request. If the final bill is at least 400 dollars more than the estimate, the client can use a federal patient-provider dispute resolution process. Many states add their own price-transparency rules. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: Tell uninsured and self-pay clients that they can get a good faith estimate, for example with a notice in the office, on the website and when they ask about cost.

Give the estimate in writing when a service is scheduled at least three business days ahead, or when a client asks for one. CMS guidance sets the deadlines, which depend on how far ahead the service is scheduled.

The estimate lists the expected items and services with their expected charges and diagnosis or service codes where used. For ongoing therapy, CMS guidance allows one estimate to cover a series of recurring sessions for a limited period.
If the bill exceeds the estimate by 400 dollars or more, the client can start patient-provider dispute resolution with CMS.
The estimate is a billing document: share only what is needed and keep it with the client's record under your usual privacy safeguards.
whatToDo: Add good faith estimate language to your intake and fee policy, and train staff who schedule appointments.
Use CMS's model notice and estimate templates, and update the estimate when the plan changes.
Keep a copy of each estimate with the client's records for the retention period your state and payers require.
Check your state's price-transparency or surprise-billing laws as well as the federal rule.
Consult a healthcare attorney or your licensing board's guidance if you are unsure how the rules apply to your practice.
